Juvenile Xenotilapia sima in the littoral zone of Lake Tanganyika typically begin exogenous feeding after the yolk-sac larva undergoes complete yolk absorption. Newly emerged prolarvae possess a meager wet weight at birth of only 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams], reflecting the modest provisioning of the small, demersal egg. This initial mass is considerably lower than that reported for many other cichlids of comparable egg diameter. As the growing juvenile develops, it undergoes a pronounced growth trajectory that ultimately leads to an asymptotic adult size. Field records indicate that the ultimate total length attained by this substrate-spawning cichlid reaches 16.4 centimeters [Li = 16.4 centimeters], a dimension consistent with its ecological role as a benthic forager. The species exhibits a relatively moderate body plan, with reproductively mature individuals tending to be substantially smaller than the maximum recorded size. Data collected from multiple expeditions suggest that this length represents the upper limit of somatic growth under natural conditions, with very few individuals exceeding this threshold in the wild.

The onset of reproductive capability in Xenotilapia sima is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body length rather than a fixed chronological age. Published accounts indicate that the total length at puberty for this species is approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters], a milestone that corresponds with the development of functional gonads. At this size, individuals typically exhibit a wet weight at puberty of about 39.3 grams [Wwp = about 39.3 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for Lake Tanganyika cichlids. This body mass at maturity is considerably less than the ultimate wet weight that the species can achieve, which has been estimated at 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams] for fully grown adults. The disparity between mass at puberty and asymptotic mass suggests that a significant portion of somatic growth occurs after the initiation of gametogenesis. This pattern is common among iteroparous fish that continue to invest in body size increments while simultaneously allocating resources toward repeated spawning events over multiple breeding seasons.

Reproductive output in Xenotilapia sima has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At this thermal regime, gravid females produce a modest clutch of 40 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 40 eggs per spawning event], deposited onto a carefully prepared substrate, and typically complete a single spawning per year [F_R_i = single spawning per year]. This low per-event fecundity and annual frequency reflect the substantial parental investment typical of substrate-guarding cichlids, where egg size and post-fertilization care limit overall output. The values were corroborated by comparison with reproductive data from the closely related Mylochromis anaphyrmus, which exhibits a similar demographic strategy.

Longevity data for Xenotilapia sima suggest a moderately extended lifespan, consistent with the slow life-history pace of many Lake Tanganyika endemics. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species under stable aquarium conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], a duration that allows for multiple reproductive cycles across the adult phase. This value is notable when compared to smaller, fast-living lacustrine species that rarely exceed two to three years. The ability to persist for half a decade or more likely facilitates the accumulation of breeding experience and the repeated production of offspring cohorts. Senescence in captive individuals typically manifests as a gradual decline in spawning frequency and a deterioration of body condition in the final year of life. Field-based estimates from mark-recapture studies in the southern basin of Lake Tanganyika support these aquarium-derived figures, indicating that natural mortality rates are low enough to permit a substantial proportion of adults to reach advanced ages.

Comparisons among Lake Tanganyika cichlids reveal that the life-history strategy of Xenotilapia sima occupies an intermediate position along the fast-slow continuum. The species achieves an adult body mass of 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams] at 16.4 centimeters [Li = 16.4 centimeters] in total length, placing it within the size range typical of benthic-feeding lamprologines. Its mass at puberty, measured at 39.3 grams [Wwp = 39.3 grams] when individuals reach 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters] in total length, represents approximately one-third of the ultimate mass, a reproductive threshold similar to that observed in congeners. The wet weight at birth of 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams] underscores the relatively small offspring size compared to the asymptotic adult mass. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the species achieves a maximum reproductive output of approximately 0.11 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 0.11 offspring per day] and a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years], reflecting a strategy that balances moderate fecundity with extended parental care and delayed senescence.
